claims.claim: Use a 60-second device show-and-tell exit check in which each child runs the name badge and says which MakeCode block made their chosen output appear, so the teacher can observe both a working program and block-to-behaviour reasoning.

For the emotion-badge lesson, have pairs demonstrate one input-output interaction and give a spoken peer prompt such as “What did you press or shake, and what did the micro:bit do?”, keeping assessment observable and low-stakes.

Use a quick gallery walk in which each learner shows their step counter, resets it, and explains why the variable starts at a known value; this directly checks the session’s stated teacher emphasis on initialization.
Close the step-counter session with a one-question oral exit ticket—“Which block changes the number after a movement?”—and accept pointing to the block or demonstrating it as alternatives to writing.

For rock-paper-scissors, use a two-person demo check: one learner shakes the micro:bit while the other predicts the possible outcomes and then describes how the program makes the choice, allowing assessment through demonstration and peer talk.

Across these short introductory MakeCode sessions, use brief Think/Create/Evaluate/Share moments to collect spoken explanations and visible device behaviour during the build rather than adding a separate written quiz at the end.
